Eli Orne, a freshman at the University of New Hampshire in Durham, said he would worry that open access to guns on campus would raise the risk of students committing suicide. State Rep. Samuel Farrington, R-Rochester, a University of New Hampshire student who sponsored a bill to allow students, staff and visitors at all public colleges in the state to carry weapons, said the legislation would not turn New Hampshire campuses into the “Wild, Wild West.” Eli Orne, a freshman at the University of New Hampshire in Durham, said he would worry that open access to guns on campus would raise the risk of students committing suicide. Personal liberty squared off against concern over higher education safety during what may have been the final public hearing Tuesday on sweeping legislation (HB 1793) to allow students, staff and visitors to carry weapons on all public college campuses in the state. State Rep. Samuel Farrington, R-Rochester, a University of New Hampshire student who sponsored the bill, faced a flurry of questions from Republican senators on the Senate Judiciary Committee who questioned whether the bill was too loosely drawn. Farrington said he’d be open to amendments to ensure guns inside a dorm were placed inside a locked box and that colleges clearly had the authority to criminally punish anyone who was impaired on campus and was carrying a weapon. At the same time, Farrington said the principle of letting students possess guns anywhere so they can defend themselves was to him non-negotiable. “Right now, they are stripped — adults, students, faculty, professors — of their natural rights,” Farrington said. “Individuals have a natural right to defend themselves with a firearm.” The presidents of the three public colleges at Durham, Keene and Plymouth, along with their campus police executives, warned the policy could lead to more violence, suicide attempts and a chaotic scene if shots are fired. “This is not about (gun) rights; this is about common sense,” UNH Deputy Police Chief Jack Dalton said at a rally outside the State House before the hearing. “Now we could have 14-15 people running in different directions, all of them with weapons and people shouting, ‘That’s the shooter.’” UNH President Elizabeth Chilton urged the Senate to send the bill off for more study. “New Hampshire has some of the safest college campuses in the country and there is no evidence that this bill will make it any safer,” Chilton said. Rep. Robert Lynn, R-Windham, a retired Supreme Court chief justice, said gun control advocates warned of New Hampshire becoming the “Wild, Wild West” when the Republican-led Legislature in 2017 adopted constitutional carry that allows legally eligible adults to possess a concealed weapon. “All those fears proved to be unfounded back then and I suspect they would be again if we pass this,” Lynn said. Eli Orne, a UNH freshman studying to be a clinical psychologist, said allowing students to have loaded guns would put many young people at risk of harming themselves. “I’ve known so many students, including myself, who have gone through mental health struggles transitioning from high school to the college environment,” Orne said. Committee Chairman Bill Gannon, R-Sandown, and Vice Chairman Daryl Abbas, R-Salem, test-marketed potential amendments such as preventing open carry by a student in class, restricting gun carrying inside dorms and adopting stiff penalties for anyone drunk with a gun on campus. “Can you tell me which amendments you could support?” Abbas asked more than one witness during several hours of testimony. Rep. Valerie McDonnell, R-Salem, said she preferred the original bill, but would not oppose the Senate adopting “time, place and manner restrictions” regarding dangerous weapon possession everywhere on school grounds. Penny Dean, a Second Amendment advocate and lawyer, said she believed allowing women students to possess guns would reduce the incidence of rape on campuses. A UNH Student Senate survey of 2,300 students found 81% strongly opposed the bill. State Rep. Samuel Farrington, R-Rochester, a University of New Hampshire student who sponsored a bill to allow students, staff and visitors at all public colleges in the state to carry weapons, said the legislation would not turn New Hampshire campuses into the “Wild, Wild West.” A UNH Survey Center poll of residents statewide was more split with 49% against it, 35% for it, 13% neutral and the other 4% with no opinion. At the rally, more than 100 opponents held signs with messages including “Kids should be sitting at desks, not hiding under them,” “Colleges are places of learning, not guns,” and “Hold my beer. Campus Carry. Really?” John McKenna with the national Campaign to Keep Guns Off Campus said the House-passed bill would be the most open-ended of any in the nation in part because it would include a $10,000 fine for every violation. John Bunker, a former UNH associate dean and New Hampshire board member of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, said a 2025 study paid for by a California pro-gun control organization found students were no safer on campuses in states that had open carry than those in states without it. “The public health research is clear; this is a dangerous, reckless and unnecessary bill,” Bunker said. But Farrington cited a 2025 study from the Crime Prevention Research Center, a conservative, pro-gun advocacy group, that found in the past decade a “good guy” with a gun stopped 36% of reported mass shooting events. “These gun control measures only restrict moral upstanding citizens,” Farrington said. Next Step: The Senate committee has until April 30 to make a recommendation. Outlook: Uncertain. The Senate panel will no doubt alter it in some form, and Gov. Kelly Ayotte has yet to weigh in on it. title: From CIA Operations to Corporate Intelligence Leadership Faculty Spotlight: Angela Miller Lewis - University of New Hampshire
content: National Security Intelligence Analysis (NSIA) faculty member Angela Miller Lewis brings a rare breadth of experience to the classroom which spans CIA operations, global private sector intelligence leadership, and rigorous academic research. Her career reflects what it means to be a true scholar practitioner: someone who not only understands intelligence in theory but has lived its real world consequences across continents and industries. Angela Miller Lewis reflects on her career path, academic foundations, leadership philosophy, and what she believes future intelligence professionals need most right now. How did your experience as a Senior Targeting Officer with the CIA shape your understanding of global intelligence work? I grew up in the Midwest, and for a long time “the world out there” felt abstract — something you read about in books or saw on the news. I didn’t actually travel abroad until my twenties, and living and working overseas completely changed how I understood global events. Suddenly, intelligence wasn’t theoretical anymore. It was tied to real places, real people, and real consequences. What struck me most was how similar people are everywhere — everyone wants safety, opportunity, dignity — but how differently those needs show up depending on culture, history, and circumstance. Working alongside partners from different countries forced me to slow down my assumptions and really listen. It taught me that perspective matters, and that good intelligence depends as much on empathy and context as it does on data. That experience made the “big picture” tangible for me. I saw how decisions made in one part of the world ripple outward, affecting communities, markets, and security far beyond national borders. It’s also what shaped my approach to intelligence today: it’s not just about collecting information — it’s about making sense of complexity in a way that helps people make better decisions in the real world. What surprised you most about how intelligence functions in the private sector after moving from government roles to companies like Disney, Salesforce, and Creative Artists Agency? What surprised me most was how familiar the work itself felt — and how unfamiliar the concept of “intelligence” often was to business leaders. At its core, intelligence doesn’t really change between the public and private sectors. It’s still about making meaning from data, providing context, and helping decision-makers navigate uncertainty. You’re still supporting both operational choices and longer-term strategy. That part translated almost seamlessly. The bigger adjustment was realizing that many private-sector leaders don’t have an intuitive understanding of what intelligence can do for them. In government, decision-makers grow up with intelligence as part of the system. In business, you often have to explain — and demonstrate — its value from scratch, even though it’s incredibly useful at senior levels. Another major difference is how risk is defined. In the private sector, reputational risk carries a different weight, and financial performance and shareholder expectations are always part of the equation. That changes how intelligence is framed and delivered. You’re not just thinking about security or geopolitics — you’re also factoring in brand, markets, employees, and customers. Ultimately, it showed me how powerful intelligence can be outside government — and how much opportunity there is to help organizations use it more intentionally to make better, more informed decisions. What skills are most critical for private sector intelligence teams today, and how can NSIA students begin preparing? Two skills stand out above everything else: critical thinking and communication. We’re living in an era of information overload. Intel professionals are constantly bombarded with data from open sources, social media, internal systems, and now AI-enabled tools — and not all of it is accurate, credible, or useful. Being able to evaluate sources, understand data provenance, and separate signal from noise has never been more important. Equally important is the ability to communicate clearly and concisely. Executives have limited time and are making dozens of decisions every day. Intel professionals have to provide context quickly, highlight implications, and deliver insights in a way that actually lands. AI adds another layer. It offers incredible scale and speed, but it also amplifies the challenge of evaluation. Intel professionals need to understand how to leverage AI ethically and responsibly while maintaining analytic rigor. For NSIA students, preparation starts with building strong critical thinking habits, practicing concise writing, and getting comfortable presenting complex ideas simply. Technical skills matter — but the ability to think clearly under uncertainty and communicate with impact is what really sets professionals apart. My doctoral research examined how geopolitically focused intelligence teams operate inside large private-sector organizations — and what actually helps them succeed in complex, fast-changing environments. Using a systems theory lens, I explored how people, processes, leadership expectations, organizational culture, and decision-maker needs interact. Rather than treating intelligence as a linear cycle, I looked at it as a living system that constantly adapts. I found that successful teams tend to share common traits: strong critical thinking, alignment with decision-makers, adaptability, and clear communication — while facing challenges like unclear expectations and reactive workflows. The research reinforced that intelligence teams thrive when they’re intentionally designed to support evolving organizational needs. That work continues to shape how I teach and train analysts today. How do your academic interests shape the way you teach critical thinking? My academic interests center on how people think — especially under uncertainty. Concepts like bounded rationality and cognitive bias directly shape how I teach. Rather than presenting intelligence as a rigid checklist, I help students understand how their own minds work — where assumptions creep in and how biases influence judgment. Structured analytic techniques become tools for building better habits, not mechanical steps. Most real-world problems aren’t linear. I encourage students to embrace complexity, think in systems, and stay comfortable with uncertainty while still making judgments. Ultimately, my goal is analytical rigor paired with self-awareness — the combination that produces intelligence that actually supports decision-making. What skills matter most for NSIA students entering the intelligence field today? Strong critical thinking, communication, adaptability, and an understanding of AI are essential across both government and corporate environments. Intelligence professionals must form sound judgments under uncertainty, translate complexity into clarity, and remain flexible as technologies and environments evolve. Above all, self-awareness and resilience sustain long, successful careers in this field. What advice do you give those entering or transitioning into intelligence careers? Be curious. Do your research. Build relationships. Intelligence skills are highly transferable, but success depends on understanding context and learning how decisions are really made. Relationships accelerate growth in ways technical skills alone cannot. What excites you most about training future intelligence professionals now? We’re at an inflection point for the profession. Geopolitical uncertainty and AI are reshaping intelligence, and how we train students today will influence decisions that affect communities and organizations for years. Helping students develop integrity, curiosity, empathy, and thoughtful use of technology — alongside traditional analytic skills — is deeply meaningful. It’s not just about techniques; it’s about shaping how future leaders approach uncertainty and responsibility. Explore Our M.S. title: UNH project for major research and mixed-use community underway in Durham - New Hampshire Public Radio
content:
This story was originally produced by the Portsmouth Herald. NHPR is republishing it in partnership with the Granite State News Collaborative. University of New Hampshire officials expect the state economy will be bolstered with the development of The Edge, a massive mixed-use, research and residential community planned for the western portion of the school’s campus. In November, UNH and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration broke ground on the new 70,500-square-foot Center of Excellence for Operational Ocean and Great Lakes Mapping, The Edge’s crown jewel. Marc Eichenberger, the university’s vice president and chief business development and innovation officer, and Jennifer Miksis-Olds, the school’s interim vice president for research and innovation, reported the center should be operational and welcoming in students, faculty, scientists and industry business partners by November 2027. The cost of building the Center of Excellence for Operational Ocean and Great Lakes Mapping alone is projected to cost $34 million, said Eichenberger. The majority of the project is federally funded, with $20 million contributed by NOAA and another $5 million from the National Institute for Standards and Technology.
